label: paragraph_title
text: PEACE PROSPECTS.

label: text
text: IMPORTANT PRELIMINARY CONVERSATIONS.

label: text
text: WILL THERE BE TERMS?

label: text
text: Optimism In Canton And Hongkong.

label: text
text: Canton, June 21.

label: text
text: Mr. Eugene Chen, the acting Minister for Foreign Affairs, has again sent a representative to Shameen to discuss with the British Consul-General the question of a settlement of the "strike."—Wah-Tsz Yat-Po. (The word "strike," in Chinese is always used in relation to the boycott and really includes both the strike and boycott).

label: text
text: The Hongkong delegation has not yet proceeded to Canton. In well-informed circles, it is thought that matters of a preliminary nature will be unofficially discussed before the actual conference opens. Such conversations may relate, or may not, to the more important issues, such as the basis of settlement.

label: text
text: Even the. Canton merchants, who are in close touch with the politicians, cannot indicate whether the terms—as announced some months ago—will be stipulated, whether they will be put forward with modifications, or if a new set will be drafted. There is still a hopeful spirit.

label: text
text: "Basis of Understanding."

label: text
text: Obviously, the preliminary negotiations will have considerable bearing on the prospects of a settlement being arrived at. It is thought that if a basis of understanding can be arrived at, the success of the conference is assured, but developments are likely to hinge on the unofficial conversations.

label: text
text: Apparently, this last move by Canton cannot be associated with previous peace efforts. On June 5, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kwangtung (Nationalist). Government wrote to the Hongkong Government asking for delegates to be appointed to negotiate. On June 16, Mr. J. F. Brenan (H.M.'s Consul-General at Canton) replied on behalf of the Hongkong Government. The reply was to the effect that the Government of Hongkong considered the "industrial strike" to be a thing of the past, but delegates would be appointed to negotiate for a termination of the boycott against British goods. The Consul-General is also quoted as having expressed pleasure at the proposals (of Carton).

label: text
text: The letter from the Hongkong Government to the Consul-General, dated June 14, is mentioned as asking for information as to when the negotiations will begin. Incidentally, Mr. Brenan was informed that H.M.'s Minister at Peking had nominated him as one of the delegates. Accordingly, the Governor of Hongkong appointed the Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp and the Hon. Mr. E. R. Halifax as the other two delegates.

label: text
text: There is still a feeling of optimism in the Colony that at least a “temporary settlement”—such including the calling off of the pickets and the automatic resumption of communications and trade—will be brought about, so that a permanent understanding can then be worked for. Those who express such a view point to the reported arrest of members of the Strikers' Tribunal by the Canton Government, and the absence of news of their release or resumption of office. On the other hand, the “outdoor” pickets (i.e., “strike” representatives not in executive capacities) are still functioning with customary vigilance.

label: paragraph_title
text: PIRATE'S METHODS WITH

label: text
text: TERRIBLE VENDETTA

label: text
text: A terrible revenge is reported to have been taken by a pirate, in the Canton River delta, on strike pickets who incurred his enmity. This pirate chief is alleged to have cut off the left ear of over seventy strikers who fell into his hands, and to have put several to death.

label: text
text: Yuen Kung is the name of the pirate. His den was at Hoi Chow, in the Heungshan district. This outlaw, it is stated, had taken part in the shipping of so-called contraband (foreign goods) through the pickets' cordons. Striet vigilance had been maintained against his boats and bad blood resulted.

label: text
text:
Some days ago, Yuen fitted out a decoy in the shape of several large cargo-boats, seemingly sailing in convoy, but really in ballast.
This fleet passed a place in the Heungshan waterways, where the pickets had a station. When the strikers went out to inspect the boats, the pirates pounced on them and carried them off to their stronghold at Hoi Chow. Several pickers were shot. Every one of the others had the left ear out off.

label: text
text: Those who escaped returned to Canton to tell the story. On the application of the strike executive committee, a military punitive expedition was sent against Yuen but he had already deserted his den and had gone into the Shuntak silk district when the troops arrived.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE SOUTH-WEST.

label: paragraph_title
text: POSSIBILITIES IN CHINA POLITICS.

label: text
text: WARLORDS ON MOVE

label: text
text: It is expected that the General-Issimo headquarters in Canton (of General Chang Kai-shek) will be established in a week.—"Wah Tsz Yat Po." (This step, as explained by the "China Mail" correspondent, will give General Chang, the actual position of military chief of the whole province and of its capital.) News from a reliable source is that neighbouring warlords of Canton are still planning to extend their scope, such action having great influence on the position of the Kuomintang. Government in Kwangtung.

label: text
text: General Tang Chi-yao and ex-Inspector General Li Yung-ting are stated to be planning an alliance. General Tang has ruled Yunnan province for some years. A threat to invade Canton last year was baulked by General Fan Shek-Bang (who withdrew his mercenaries from Canton) but Fan's following has now practically dispersed and is non-effective. Tang is reported as not being averse to a treaty with Lu, to safeguard his own interests, under the declared policy of Wu Pei-fu, of provincial cooperative automony in the southwest of China.

label: text
text: Lu Yung-ting once held both Kwangtung and Kwangsi. He is now said to be calling on his former subordinates to raise his standard in Kwangsi province, which is under the control of two generals who profess allegiance to Canton. Lu desires Tang's goodwill so that he can regain a footing in Kwangsi. He is believed to be favoured by Wu Pei-fu and his sending of a former national M.P. into Yunnan is taken as indicative of political possibilities in the near future.

label: text
text: When the Kowloon 'Residents' Association circulated amongst its members, a questionnaire with regard to opinions on the desirability or otherwise of continuing restriction of rents, there was also a question as to whether, in the event of the Government withdrawing restriction (as they now definitely have done), residents favoured the institution of a Fair Rents Board.

label: text
text: In view of the lapsing of the Rents-Restriction Ordinance at the end of this month, a “China Mail” representative made enquiries this morning as to whether the question of the Fair Rents Board would be pressed by the Kowloon Residents’ Association. He was informed that although no meeting had yet been held on the question, on the strength of the referendum the Association would be petitioning the Government for the institution of such a Board.

label: text
text: On the general rents question, it is interesting to note that Sir Shou-son Chow and Dr. R. H. Kotewall, Chinese members of the Legislative Council, have jointly issued a letter to the Chinese landlords advising them to be fair to their tenants when the restriction Ordinances lapses.

label: text

label: text
text: Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, replied, referring to his answer on June 14: He added that he was still in close consultation with the British Minister in Peking as regards measures to meet the attack on the salt administration in Tientain. Every effort was being made to investigate the recent murders of British subjects in order to ascertain the responsibility.

label: text
text: Asked whether he would suspend the tariff negotiations until our Treaty rights were respected, Sir Austen Chamberlain said that the tariff negotiations were being conducted by several Powers. It was most desirable, if possible, that all the Powers should act in harmony. —Reuter.

label: text

Peking, June 15.
The Cabinet announces receipt of a telegram from Marshal Sun Chuan-fang stating that "he is willing to release certain Kiangsu salt revenues.

label: paragraph_title
text: SUN AND SALT REVENUE

label: text
text: The position is that by the 1925 agreement the Salt Administration should collect all the Kiangsu salt revenues and pay Marshal Sun 50 per cent., but last April Marshal Sun forbade transfer of the salt revenues to Shanghai. Dr. W. W. Yen recently telegraphed to the Marshal requesting him to release the salt funds and the Marshal informed the Cabinet that he was willing to do so as regards collections to the end of May. He emphasised that his action was largely a matter of personal friendship for Dr. Yen and clearly stated that the question of Peking drawing the salt funds for periods after May must be referred to him.

label: text
text: The transfer of the salt funds from the collectorates to Shanghai will take about ten days and, therefore, no funds have yet reached the group banks at Shanghai. The period involved will be less than two months and the usual 50 per cent. will be returned to Marshal Sun. — Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: LOCAL RENTALS.

label: paragraph_title
text: IS A "FAIR RENTS BOARD" NECESSARY.

label: text
text: TENANT'S PLEA.

label: text
text: (To the Editor of the China Mail.)

label: text
text: Sir,—Not every house owner in this Colony is a bona fide landlord who buys property for investment. There are some who still hold lots of property because they were “caught” when the slump came. It would only be human if they were to exploit the situation, when the Rents Ordinance expires on June 30. Their natural course would be to threaten demolition, or give a month's notice to quit, or increase the rentals as much as possible—and then try to sell out on the artificially inflated value.

label: text
text: Then again there are landlords who are very bitter over what has transpired during the last few years. I admit that in the majority of cases, tenants were to blame for tactless handling. More than one owner have indicated that they will serve notice if only to get their revenge back because silly tenants once flaunted the Ordinance in their faces.

label: text
text: To protect the innocent, it has been submitted that Fair Rents Board should be instituted. With all due respect I predict that the agitation for such a body will become intolerable. A rents tribunal has worked satisfactorily in other colonies and should do so here. There ought to be no hardship for owners, as each case will be dealt with on individual merits. Landlords will still be at liberty to throw occupants out, to demolish and reconstruct, to raise rents, to re-enter into possession themselves and there need be no appeal from them. A tenant who feels that he is being exploited can obtain justice. Values are fixed for assessment of rates and a tribunal can take the Government figures for guidance, instead of wasting time in hearing evidence and arguments. Capital will not be scared away—for fear of alleged restriction on legitimate enterprise—as fair returns will be granted by a Rents Board. The name itself assures both sides of a square deal and not a one-sided ruling.

label: text
text: In conclusion I would, Sir, point out that the sudden abandonment of all restriction will tend to the opposite extreme. I anticipate the landlords' reply to this—that ample notice has been given by the Government. Just as it was claimed when the Ordinance suddenly came into force, that landlords were unduly penalised, so now they will make—not in every instance—unwarranted profits of those who must rent houses. Control came in easy stages—as witness the many amendments to the Rents Ordinance. Decontrol should, therefore, come also in easy stages. The best answer to that, and the greatest good for the greatest number, lies in the immediate establishment of a Rents Board.

label: text
text: Should the Government not lend ear, I advise every tenant to give full publicity to facts, as soon as he receives that nightmare of a letter from the landlord.

label: text
text:
Yours, etc.,
FLAT DWELLER.
Hongkong, June 22, 1926.

label: paragraph_title
text: Motor Smash Sequel.

label: text
text: An accident in which a motor car crashed into the wall of the Hongkong Electric Company's premises at North Point on June 14, causing severe injuries to four passengers, was recalled before Major C. Willson when the driver was charged on two counts of negligent driving and using a private car for public hire.

label: text
text:
Sub-Inspector Alexander said that defendant accosted a number of Chinese ladies and children coming out of the Sincere Company's shop and offered to drive them to their home in Shaukiwan for $2. At the scene of the accident, which was a controlled area, defendant was driving at the rate of about 20 miles an hour and, in attempting to avoid a lorry, the driver of which indicated that he was going to stop, the car crashed into the wall. The Inspector explained that a civil action for damages consequent on injuries received by the passengers might probably arise at a later date when the owner of the car was found.
Defendant admitted the first charge and on the other he said he took the passengers to be friends of his employer. He was fined $60
